title: An old solar cell still has something to give.
label: Lasers, recycling & automation
opening: A worn-out solar cell is still full of useful material. The question that got me interested was simple: could a laser help us get that material back, without destroying everything around it?
body: I developed ways to recover silver from silicon and CIGS solar cells, either as larger pieces or as tiny particles. That meant choosing a laser, changing the processing conditions, and looking closely at what came off and what was left behind. I also worked on removing the polymer backsheet from a module while keeping its glass and silicon intact.

Then came a very practical problem: broken cells don’t arrive in neat, identical shapes. I used image segmentation and Python to find the metal contacts in a picture and turn them into paths the laser could follow. My childhood interest in making things move more or less found its natural habitat.
lesson: Getting a material off is only half the job. Knowing what you recovered, what you damaged, and whether you can repeat it is the other half.

title: Before testing a material, sometimes you have to grow it.
label: Single-crystal growth & battery materials
opening: Working with materials at IIT Delhi took me a step further back in the story: how do you make the sample you want to study in the first place?
body: My work involved single-crystal growth, pulsed laser deposition, vacuum systems, and measurements of structure and electronic properties. It was hands-on work: prepare a sample, check what actually formed, and work out which part of the process needs another try.

I’m also a co-author on a study of MoSeTe as a possible anode for sodium-ion batteries. Sodium is abundant, which makes the search for suitable battery materials especially interesting. The study looked at both the material’s structure and how it behaved during charging and discharging.
lesson: A good first result is an invitation to keep testing. How a material behaves over repeated cycles matters just as much.

title: A very thin film. Quite a lot to figure out.
label: Transparent conducting oxide films
opening: Some materials need to let light through and carry electricity at the same time. That combination led me into transparent conducting oxide films during my MSc at IIT Ropar.
body: I made antimony-doped tin oxide films using thermal evaporation followed by controlled oxidation. Then I checked their crystal structure, how much light passed through, and how easily current flowed.
The interesting part was connecting those measurements back to how the film had been made. A layer that looks unremarkable on a piece of glass can have a very different story once you measure it.
lesson: Making the film and measuring the film belong in the same conversation. Otherwise, it is very easy to optimize the wrong thing.

title: What can a camera see when there’s barely any light?
label: Low-light imaging & scientific computing
opening: In dim light, a camera has very little signal to work with. Noise starts to compete with the scene itself. I’m interested in understanding that noise and how we evaluate attempts to recover the image.
body: My work brings together RAW image analysis, statistical noise modeling, Python, and image-restoration evaluation. I work with the measurements behind an image as well as the image we eventually look at.
This is another place where my physics and programming interests meet. It is also a useful reminder that a prettier picture and a more faithful measurement are different questions.
lesson: Start by understanding the noise. Then ask whether an apparent improvement survives a careful, controlled comparison.
